text: Picking up where Lesson 34 left off, with the sketch, now it's time to build the real tables and lock down what matters. Two tables, and one deliberate security decision.

x_acme_eqchk_equipment is a lookup table — asset_tag, equipment_name, category, equipment_condition, and availability. It doesn't extend task, because it isn't a workflow record. x_acme_eqchk_request does extend task, adding equipment, requested_for, approved_by, due_date, checkout_date, and return_date on top of everything task already provides — state, assigned_to, opened_by. A reference field, equipment, joins the two.

That reference field is the same dot-walk pattern used throughout this course. A request record never duplicates the equipment's name or condition — it just stores a sys_id pointing at the equipment record, and this code reads straight through that reference to get the equipment name and its current condition, with no separate lookup query needed. Keeping the data in one place also means an update to the equipment record is instantly visible from every request that references it.

Not everyone who can see an equipment record should be able to change its condition — that's a judgment call reserved for whoever actually inspects the physical item. This ACL script, on the equipment_condition field's write operation, returns true only for a custom equipment-admin role or a system admin. Everyone else sees that one field read-only, even while the rest of the form — asset tag, name, category — stays fully editable to them.

Lesson 36 builds a Script Include called EquipmentAvailabilityChecker, whose job is checking whether a piece of equipment is currently loaned out. Chapter 5's cross-scope lessons showed that Application Access controls whether code outside this scope can call it — and since nothing else in this instance has any reason to check equipment availability, it's set to this application scope only. The narrowest access that still works.
Real tables, a real reference field, and a real ACL locking down a sensitive field. Next up: the actual Business Rule, Script Include, and Client Script that make this application do something.
